name: career-technical-openquiz-embedded-data-infra
description: 按 Career OS JD 缺口补充的公开技术测评题；题干、选项和解释均直接来自 Open Quiz Commons，不新增原创题。Rust 部分仅作为嵌入式系统基础，不能替代 C/C++/RTOS 专项训练。

source.selection_basis: Career OS jobs 表的 iot-embedded、software-testing-ops、technical-support-fae、data-analysis、ai-rag 题型缺口映射

questions.title: What attribute indicates that a Rust program does not link the standard library?
questions.explanation: #[no_std] tells the compiler to not link the standard library, which is required for most embedded targets.
questions.source_text: What attribute indicates that a Rust program does not link the standard library?

questions.title: Which crate provides a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) for STM32 microcontrollers?
questions.explanation: The stm32f4xx-hal crate (and similar family-specific crates) provide HAL implementations for STM32 devices.
questions.source_text: Which crate provides a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) for STM32 microcontrollers?

questions.title: What is the typical entry point for a #[no_std] embedded program using cortex-m-rt?
questions.explanation: The cortex-m-rt crate provides the #[entry] attribute to mark the entry function, which must be diverging (!).
questions.source_text: What is the typical entry point for a #[no_std] embedded program using cortex-m-rt?

questions.title: Which command-line tool is commonly used to flash and debug ARM Cortex-M devices from Cargo?
questions.explanation: cargo-embed (installed via `cargo install cargo-embed`) provides flashing, debugging, and RTT logging for embedded targets.
questions.source_text: Which command-line tool is commonly used to flash and debug ARM Cortex-M devices from Cargo?

questions.title: What does the `cortex-m-rt` crate provide?
options: B. Startup code, vector table, and the #[entry] macro
C. A hardware abstraction layer for Cortex-M
D. An async executor for embassy
questions.explanation: cortex-m-rt supplies the minimal runtime: reset handler, vector table, and the #[entry] macro for #[no_std] programs.
questions.source_text: What does the `cortex-m-rt` crate provide?

questions.title: In embedded Rust, what is the purpose of the `#[interrupt]` attribute?
options: A. To mark a function as an interrupt handler
B. To disable interrupts for a critical section
C. To declare a peripheral register block
D. To define a memory region
questions.explanation: #[interrupt] (provided by cortex-m-rt) registers a function as an interrupt handler in the vector table.
questions.source_text: In embedded Rust, what is the purpose of the `#[interrupt]` attribute?

questions.title: Which trait from `embedded-hal` represents a digital output pin?
questions.explanation: OutputPin is the basic trait for setting a pin high or low. ToggleableOutputPin extends it with toggle().
questions.source_text: Which trait from `embedded-hal` represents a digital output pin?

questions.title: What is the typical memory map for an STM32 Cortex-M device?
questions.explanation: Most STM32 parts map Flash at 0x0800_0000 and SRAM at 0x2000_0000. The vector table is usually at the start of Flash.
questions.source_text: What is the typical memory map for an STM32 Cortex-M device?

questions.title: Which command creates a new embedded project using the cortex-m-quickstart template?
questions.explanation: cargo-generate with the cortex-m-quickstart repository sets up a ready-to-use #[no_std] project with proper memory layout.
questions.source_text: Which command creates a new embedded project using the cortex-m-quickstart template?

questions.title: What is the role of `defmt` in embedded Rust?
options: C. Deferred formatting for efficient, low-overhead logging
questions.explanation: defmt serializes log arguments on the device and formats them on the host, enabling fast logging with minimal flash/RAM usage.
questions.source_text: What is the role of `defmt` in embedded Rust?

questions.title: Which attribute marks a function as the panic handler in a #[no_std] program?
questions.explanation: #[panic_handler] (from core) defines the function called on panic; it must have signature fn(&PanicInfo) -> !.
questions.source_text: Which attribute marks a function as the panic handler in a #[no_std] program?

questions.title: What does the `heapless` crate provide?
options: A. A global heap allocator for embedded
B. Data structures that operate without a heap allocator
C. A memory protection unit driver
questions.explanation: heapless offers Vec, String, etc. backed by fixed-size arrays, avoiding the need for a heap allocator.
questions.source_text: What does the `heapless` crate provide?

questions.title: In the Embassy async framework, what is an `Executor`?
options: B. A task scheduler that runs async tasks
C. A trait for GPIO pins
questions.explanation: The Executor polls futures and manages task state, typically driven by a hardware interrupt (e.g., SysTick).
questions.source_text: In the Embassy async framework, what is an `Executor`?

questions.title: Which cargo subcommand flashes firmware when using `cargo-embed`?
questions.explanation: `cargo embed` builds the project and flashes it to the target via a debug probe, then opens an RTT console.
questions.source_text: Which cargo subcommand flashes firmware when using `cargo-embed`?

questions.title: What does the `#[rtic::app]` attribute do?
options: A. Defines an RTIC application with tasks, resources, and interrupts
B. Marks a function as real-time critical
C. Enables the Rust compiler's real-time optimizations
D. Imports the RTIC hardware abstraction layer
questions.explanation: #[rtic::app] is a procedural macro that generates the scaffolding for a Real-Time Interrupt-driven Concurrency (RTIC) application.
questions.source_text: What does the `#[rtic::app]` attribute do?

questions.title: In Rust, what does the ownership system primarily help with?
options: A. Memory safety without a garbage collector
questions.explanation: Rust's ownership system ensures memory safety and prevents data races without needing a garbage collector.
questions.source_text: In Rust, what does the ownership system primarily help with?

questions.title: In Rust, which keyword is used to create a reference to a value without taking ownership?
questions.explanation: The '&' symbol is used to create an immutable reference to a value without taking ownership.
questions.source_text: In Rust, which keyword is used to create a reference to a value without taking ownership?

questions.title: What happens if you try to have two mutable references to the same data simultaneously in Rust?
options: B. Compiler error due to borrowing rules
questions.explanation: Rust's borrowing rules prevent having two mutable references to the same data at the same time to ensure safety.
questions.source_text: What happens if you try to have two mutable references to the same data simultaneously in Rust?

questions.title: What does the term 'borrowing' mean in Rust?
options: B. Creating a reference to a value without taking ownership
C. Copying the data to a new variable
D. Cloning data using a method
questions.explanation: Borrowing means creating references (& or &mut) to data without transferring ownership.
questions.source_text: What does the term 'borrowing' mean in Rust?

questions.title: Which of these can be mutated in Rust?
options: C. The original data if only borrowed immutably
D. Ownership transferred to a function
questions.explanation: Only mutable references (&mut T) allow mutation. Immutable references (&T) do not permit mutation.
questions.source_text: Which of these can be mutated in Rust?

questions.title: What does the 'move' keyword do in Rust closures?
options: A. Moves ownership of captured variables into the closure
questions.explanation: 'move' forces the closure to take ownership of captured variables instead of borrowing them.
questions.source_text: What does the 'move' keyword do in Rust closures?

questions.title: Which trait must a type implement to be safely copied rather than moved in Rust?
questions.explanation: 'Copy' types implement implicit copying instead of moving, usually for simple scalar types.
questions.source_text: Which trait must a type implement to be safely copied rather than moved in Rust?

questions.title: What is the lifetime specifier used for in Rust?
options: B. Describing scope of references to ensure validity
C. Annotating ownership transfer between threads
questions.explanation: Lifetimes help the compiler check that references remain valid and prevent dangling references.
questions.source_text: What is the lifetime specifier used for in Rust?

questions.title: What does borrowing with '&mut' mean in Rust?
questions.explanation: '&mut' is a mutable reference that allows modifying the borrowed data.
questions.source_text: What does borrowing with '&mut' mean in Rust?

questions.title: Why can Rust prevent data races at compile time?
options: A. Because of ownership and borrowing rules
B. Because it uses garbage collection
D. Because all data is immutable
questions.explanation: Rust's ownership and borrowing rules enforced at compile time eliminate data races.
questions.source_text: Why can Rust prevent data races at compile time?

questions.title: In Rust, which type is commonly used for error handling that can represent either success or failure?
questions.explanation: The Result<T, E> type is used to represent either a success (Ok) or failure (Err) outcome in Rust.
questions.source_text: In Rust, which type is commonly used for error handling that can represent either success or failure?

questions.title: What does the 'Ok' variant of Result<T, E> represent in Rust?
options: C. A successful computation with value T
questions.explanation: 'Ok' indicates success and holds a value of type T.
questions.source_text: What does the 'Ok' variant of Result<T, E> represent in Rust?

questions.title: What is the purpose of the 'Err' variant in Rust's Result type?
options: B. Represents an error and holds error information
questions.explanation: 'Err' means an error occurred and holds an error value of type E.
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of the 'Err' variant in Rust's Result type?

questions.title: Which Rust macro can be used to explicitly cause a panic with a custom message?
questions.explanation: The panic!() macro triggers a panic, optionally with a custom error message.
questions.source_text: Which Rust macro can be used to explicitly cause a panic with a custom message?

questions.title: What does the '?' operator do in Rust when used after a Result-returning expression?
options: B. Unwraps the Result and panics on Err
C. Returns the Err early from the function, or unwraps Ok
D. Converts the Result to an Option
questions.explanation: The '?' operator propagates the Err early or unwraps the Ok value.
questions.source_text: What does the '?' operator do in Rust when used after a Result-returning expression?

questions.title: Which trait must an error type implement to be usable with the standard Rust error handling ecosystem?
questions.explanation: The std::error::Error trait indicates a type is an error and supports interoperability.
questions.source_text: Which trait must an error type implement to be usable with the standard Rust error handling ecosystem?

questions.title: In Rust, which method converts an Option<T> into a Result<T, E> by supplying an error if None?
questions.explanation: ok_or() converts Option<T> to Result<T, E> by providing an error value for None.
questions.source_text: In Rust, which method converts an Option<T> into a Result<T, E> by supplying an error if None?

questions.title: How would you recover or transform the error value in a Result<T, E>?
questions.explanation: map_err() allows you to map or transform the error value in a Result.
questions.source_text: How would you recover or transform the error value in a Result<T, E>?

questions.title: What is the difference between unwrap() and expect() on a Result in Rust?
options: A. unwrap() returns Option, expect() returns Result
B. unwrap() panics with default message, expect() panics with provided message
C. unwrap() handles errors gracefully, expect() ignores errors
questions.explanation: unwrap() panics with default message on Err; expect() panics with a custom message.
questions.source_text: What is the difference between unwrap() and expect() on a Result in Rust?

questions.title: What is the behavior of Rust's panic! macro when invoked?
options: B. Gracefully logs the error and continues
C. Terminates the current thread by unwinding or aborting
questions.explanation: panic! macro causes thread termination either by unwinding stack or aborting.
questions.source_text: What is the behavior of Rust's panic! macro when invoked?

questions.title: Which approach is preferred in Rust for recoverable errors?
questions.explanation: Result<T, E> is preferred for recoverable errors to handle them gracefully.
questions.source_text: Which approach is preferred in Rust for recoverable errors?

questions.title: What is the role of the 'anyhow' crate in Rust error handling?
options: A. Provides a Result alias for easier error propagation
B. Simplifies error handling by providing a generic error type
C. Cause program to panic on errors
questions.explanation: anyhow provides a convenient generic error type to simplify error management.
questions.source_text: What is the role of the 'anyhow' crate in Rust error handling?

questions.title: How can you chain errors to preserve context in Rust?
options: A. Using the chain_err() method from custom crates
questions.explanation: Many crates provide chain_err() or context methods to add error context to Result errors.
questions.source_text: How can you chain errors to preserve context in Rust?

questions.title: What is the difference between panic and Result in Rust?
options: A. panic is for recoverable errors, Result is for unrecoverable errors
B. panic aborts thread or program, Result handles recoverable outcomes
D. panic returns an error code
questions.explanation: panic leads to thread abort, Result is used for recoverable error handling.
questions.source_text: What is the difference between panic and Result in Rust?

questions.title: Which method converts a Result<T, E> into an Option<T>, discarding the error?
questions.explanation: ok() converts Result to Option, yielding Some(T) if Ok or None if Err.
questions.source_text: Which method converts a Result<T, E> into an Option<T>, discarding the error?

questions.title: Which Python library is most commonly used to connect to PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: psycopg (psycopg2/psycopg3) is the most widely used and mature PostgreSQL adapter for Python.
questions.source_text: Which Python library is most commonly used to connect to PostgreSQL?

questions.title: Which command is used to install psycopg2 using pip?
questions.explanation: psycopg2 can be installed using pip install psycopg2 (or psycopg2-binary for quick setups).
questions.source_text: Which command is used to install psycopg2 using pip?

questions.title: Which PostgreSQL feature is NOT available in SQLite?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports advanced data types like JSONB, which SQLite does not fully implement.
questions.source_text: Which PostgreSQL feature is NOT available in SQLite?

questions.title: How do you create a connection using psycopg?
questions.explanation: psycopg.connect() establishes a connection to a PostgreSQL database.
questions.source_text: How do you create a connection using psycopg?

questions.title: Which placeholder syntax does psycopg use for parameterized queries?
questions.explanation: psycopg uses %s placeholders regardless of the underlying data type.
questions.source_text: Which placeholder syntax does psycopg use for parameterized queries?

questions.title: Why are parameterized queries important in PostgreSQL applications?
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries protect applications from SQL injection by separating SQL logic from data.
questions.source_text: Why are parameterized queries important in PostgreSQL applications?

questions.title: Which method is used to retrieve a cursor from a PostgreSQL connection?
questions.explanation: cursor() creates a cursor object used to execute SQL statements.
questions.source_text: Which method is used to retrieve a cursor from a PostgreSQL connection?

questions.title: What is the default transaction behavior in PostgreSQL connections?
questions.explanation: By default, PostgreSQL connections require an explicit commit() to persist changes.
questions.source_text: What is the default transaction behavior in PostgreSQL connections?

questions.title: Which PostgreSQL feature helps ensure data consistency under concurrent access?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL uses MVCC to allow concurrent reads and writes without blocking.
questions.source_text: Which PostgreSQL feature helps ensure data consistency under concurrent access?

questions.title: Which command safely closes a PostgreSQL database connection in Python?
questions.explanation: close() releases the database connection and associated resources.
questions.source_text: Which command safely closes a PostgreSQL database connection in Python?

questions.title: What is the most fundamental difference between the `requests` library and `aiohttp`?
options: A. Requests is faster for single requests
B. Requests is synchronous/blocking, while aiohttp is asynchronous/non-blocking
D. Requests is part of the standard library
questions.explanation: `requests` blocks the execution of the program until the server responds, whereas `aiohttp` allows the program to handle other tasks while waiting for the network.
questions.source_text: What is the most fundamental difference between the `requests` library and `aiohttp`?

questions.title: Which `aiohttp` object is recommended to be created once and reused for multiple requests to the same host?
questions.explanation: Reusing a `ClientSession` allows for connection pooling and provides a significant performance boost compared to creating a new session for every request.
questions.source_text: Which `aiohttp` object is recommended to be created once and reused for multiple requests to the same host?

questions.title: In `requests`, how do you perform a POST request with JSON data?
questions.explanation: The `json` parameter in `requests.post()` automatically encodes a Python dictionary to a JSON string and sets the `Content-Type` header to `application/json`.
questions.source_text: In `requests`, how do you perform a POST request with JSON data?

questions.title: In `aiohttp`, what is the correct syntax for making a GET request and reading the text response?
options: A. resp = await session.get(url); text = resp.text()
B. async with session.get(url) as resp: text = await resp.text()
D. with session.get(url) as resp: text = resp.text()
questions.explanation: `aiohttp` uses asynchronous context managers (`async with`) and requires the `.text()` method to be awaited because reading the body is an IO operation.
questions.source_text: In `aiohttp`, what is the correct syntax for making a GET request and reading the text response?

questions.title: What happens if you use `requests.get()` inside an `async def` coroutine managed by `asyncio`?
options: C. It blocks the entire event loop, stopping all other concurrent tasks
D. It executes in a background thread by default
questions.explanation: Because `requests` is synchronous, it will block the thread it is running in, which in an `asyncio` app is the thread running the event loop.
questions.source_text: What happens if you use `requests.get()` inside an `async def` coroutine managed by `asyncio`?

questions.title: Which library is better suited for a script that needs to download 1,000 images simultaneously?
questions.explanation: `aiohttp` is designed for high-concurrency scenarios, allowing many requests to be 'in-flight' at once without the overhead of thousands of threads.
questions.source_text: Which library is better suited for a script that needs to download 1,000 images simultaneously?

questions.title: How does `requests` handle connection pooling by default?
options: C. It creates a pool for every global `get()` call
D. It uses the operating system's global pool
questions.explanation: A `requests.Session` object provides connection pooling (via urllib3), allowing for the reuse of the underlying TCP connection.
questions.source_text: How does `requests` handle connection pooling by default?

questions.title: Which `aiohttp` method is used to retrieve binary content (like an image) from a response?
questions.explanation: In `aiohttp`, `await resp.read()` is used to get the response body as bytes, whereas `await resp.text()` is for strings.
questions.source_text: Which `aiohttp` method is used to retrieve binary content (like an image) from a response?

questions.title: In `requests`, how do you check if a request failed (e.g., a 404 or 500 error) without checking the status code manually?
questions.explanation: `raise_for_status()` will raise an `HTTPError` if the status code indicates a client or server error (4xx or 5xx).
questions.source_text: In `requests`, how do you check if a request failed (e.g., a 404 or 500 error) without checking the status code manually?

questions.title: What is the `aiohttp` equivalent of the `requests` timeout parameter `timeout=5`?
options: D. Both B and C are valid ways to handle timeouts
questions.explanation: `aiohttp` uses a `ClientTimeout` object for fine-grained control, but `asyncio.wait_for` is also a common way to wrap any awaitable with a timeout.
questions.source_text: What is the `aiohttp` equivalent of the `requests` timeout parameter `timeout=5`?

questions.title: Which library would be more 'Pythonic' for a simple, linear script that fetches one page and parses it?
questions.explanation: `requests` is famous for its simple, human-readable API. If concurrency isn't needed, the overhead of setting up an event loop for `aiohttp` is usually unnecessary.
questions.source_text: Which library would be more 'Pythonic' for a simple, linear script that fetches one page and parses it?

questions.title: In `aiohttp`, why is it important to call `await session.close()` or use a context manager?
options: A. To delete the temporary cookies
B. To properly release the underlying connections in the pool
C. To signal the server to shut down
D. To save the history to disk
questions.explanation: Failing to close an `aiohttp` session can lead to unclosed connection warnings and resource leaks in long-running applications.
questions.source_text: In `aiohttp`, why is it important to call `await session.close()` or use a context manager?
